Consistency.justification: The proposal is strongly aligned with the supplied research idea. It includes all central elements: hypergraph construction, role-aware and adjacency-aware representations, state-space modeling, transformer-like learned fusion, hypergraph convolution, residual connections, over-smoothing mitigation, and node classification. The experiments and ablations directly test the stated hypothesis about combining role and adjacency channels through SSMs. The main limitation is a slight shift in emphasis from the original HGMN idea toward a more ambitious continuous-time incidence-axis interpretation, which is not yet defined rigorously enough to establish that it is fully consistent with the claimed mechanism. The discussion of related work is relevant, but it relies on broad comparisons rather than a systematic account of precisely how each component differs from the closest model.

Clarity.justification: The motivation, high-level architecture, datasets, baselines, metrics, ablations, and risks are presented in a logical and understandable manner. The separation into adjacency and role channels is especially clear. However, several central operational details remain ambiguous. It is not clear exactly what constitutes the SSM sequence at each node, how incidence-driven propagation states are batched, how the role channel is propagated, or whether cross-attention operates only between two representations of the same node or globally across nodes and hyperedges. The terms continuous-time state evolution, incidence-driven index, propagation axis, and HiPPO-like positional encoding are used without precise definitions. The proposal also alternates between several possible role encoders rather than committing to a primary formulation. These ambiguities prevent the method from being immediately reproducible.

Novelty.justification: The incidence-propagation interpretation of SSM processing, explicit separation of role and adjacency channels, and adaptive cross-channel fusion form a potentially useful new combination. Applying an SSM over successive hypergraph propagation states rather than merely inserting an SSM block into a hypergraph network could be a meaningful distinction if formalized and validated. Nevertheless, nearly every individual ingredient already exists in adjacent literature: hypergraph convolution, structural role embeddings, dual-view processing, SSM-based long-range modeling, attention or gated fusion, and residual anti-over-smoothing mechanisms. More importantly, the supplied core idea already specifies the same combination of role-aware representations, hypergraphs, state-space modeling, and transformer-like fusion. The proposal therefore appears primarily incremental and compositional rather than groundbreaking. Its novelty also depends heavily on an asserted distinction from the 2025 SSM-hypergraph paper that is not established through a detailed technical comparison.

Soundness.justification: The proposal rests on plausible foundations and includes sensible controls, residual connections, normalization, statistical testing, robustness evaluation, and extensive ablations. However, the central mathematical mechanism is insufficiently specified and contains a likely dimensional inconsistency. Under the common convention that the incidence matrix H has shape number-of-nodes by number-of-hyperedges, H transpose times H acts on hyperedge features, not node features, so the stated update H transpose H x is invalid when x is a node-feature matrix; node-to-node propagation would instead involve an appropriately normalized H H transpose operator, while bipartite propagation would alternate node-to-hyperedge and hyperedge-to-node maps. The claim that the repeated incidence multiplications can be computed in closed form through SSM convolution with the propagation kernel is not derived and may conflate convolution over an ordered time axis with powers of a graph operator. It is also unclear why HiPPO positional encodings are appropriate for an unordered hypergraph or how permutation equivariance is guaranteed. The over-smoothing hypothesis is plausible, but residual connections alone do not demonstrate that the SSM avoids over-smoothing. A rigorous operator definition, complexity analysis, stability argument, and permutation-equivariance proof or justification are needed.

Feasibility.justification: Most components can be implemented using current sparse hypergraph operators, diagonal or low-rank SSM libraries, structural-feature extraction, and small attention modules. The proposed benchmarks and most ablations are practical. However, the plan combines many costly elements: repeated incidence propagation, storage or generation of length-L state sequences, two SSM channels, role-feature preprocessing, learnable hyperedge weights, and cross-attention. If attention is global across nodes or incidences, scalability to ogbn-arxiv, Yelp, or DBLP may be problematic; if it is only per node across two channels, it may be computationally easy but substantially less expressive than implied. Local spectral descriptors, struc2vec, and repeated hypergraph constructions also create nontrivial preprocessing costs and possible leakage concerns in transductive evaluation. Availability and reproducibility of some specialized baselines are uncertain. Feasibility would improve with explicit sparse algorithms, asymptotic time and memory bounds, a fixed role encoder, and a precise definition of the fusion scope.

Significance.justification: Long-range information propagation and over-smoothing are important problems in graph and hypergraph learning, and structural roles can provide information that local adjacency aggregation misses. A successful model that captures long-range higher-order dependencies efficiently could have meaningful value for node classification and potentially other hypergraph tasks. The planned evaluation of label sparsity, calibration, runtime, memory, and construction sensitivity broadens the practical relevance. However, the likely impact is moderated by the incremental nature of the component combination, dependence on manually constructed hypergraphs and role signatures, and the possibility that gains will be limited to datasets with strong role heterogeneity. Standard citation benchmarks may not convincingly demonstrate a need for the proposed machinery, and node classification alone limits the breadth of the contribution.

strengths: Strong alignment with the target idea and a comprehensive empirical plan covering baselines, ablations, robustness, calibration, over-smoothing, and efficiency.
Potentially valuable combination of long-range state-space processing with explicit role and adjacency channels in hypergraphs.
The proposal acknowledges major risks, including prior-art overlap, construction sensitivity, computational cost, and role-feature quality.
weaknesses: The core incidence-axis SSM mechanism is not mathematically well-defined and includes a likely incidence-matrix dimensional error.
Novelty over the supplied core idea and the closest SSM-hypergraph and role-aware methods is asserted but not demonstrated through a precise component-by-component comparison.
Permutation equivariance, the scope of cross-attention, the use of HiPPO positional information, and the claimed closed-form computation require substantial clarification.
Scalability on large datasets is uncertain because the proposal lacks explicit complexity bounds and a concrete sparse implementation plan.
